column1: # Coastlines, as closed outlines in lon,lat degrees.
# Why outlines and not a grid of characters. The world is 72x36 hexes, which is
# 2592 cells, and a hand-corrected character grid of that size is not something
# a reviewer can check by reading. An outline is: a vertex is a place, you can
# see that it is wrong, and you can move it. scripts/gen_game_data.py rasterises
# these into the hex grid and then asserts three things about the result: that
# no two ports share a hex, that every port has land in an adjoining hex, and
# that all 70 are reachable from one another by sea. A coastline that walls a
# port in, or that leaves one floating in open ocean, fails the build rather
# than shipping quietly.
# These are hand-placed from ordinary geographic knowledge at roughly 5-degree
# fidelity, which is the granularity the port coordinates come in. They are not
# derived from any dataset, so there is no licence to carry and no geospatial
# dependency to install. They are deliberately coarse: this is a chart, not a
# survey, and at one hex per 5 degrees the Baltic is two cells wide.
# Winding does not matter; the rasteriser uses an even-odd crossing test.
# Format:  name <TAB> lon,lat lon,lat ...
# One consequence of a crossing test on a coarse grid is worth knowing about,
# because it bites silently. A cell becomes land only if the cell's centre
# falls inside an outline, so anything smaller than a hex can miss every centre
# and vanish. Sri Lanka and Hispaniola did exactly that, and Colombo and Santo
# Domingo were left as harbours in open sea. Where a real island is smaller
# than 5 degrees the outline below is a box drawn around it, sized to catch one
# cell centre and no more. That is a lie about the island's size and an honest
# statement of its position, which is the trade the grid forces. Hawaii, the
# Marianas and Cape Verde are all in that category and are named for what they
# stand in for.
Africa
Eurasia
Britain
Ireland
Iceland
Scandinavia_Baltic

# Inland seas, carved out of the land above. A leading "-" subtracts.
# The Black Sea, the Red Sea and the Gulf are all narrower than the outlines
# that surround them, so painting Eurasia and Africa alone seals them shut and
# strands Azov, Trebizond, Mecca and Baghdad behind a wall of rasterised land.
# Cutting them back out is what makes those four sailable at all.
# The Sea of Okhotsk is here for the same reason but was once wrong in the
# other direction: it reached to 66N, which removed the Siberian shore along
# with the sea and left Tauisk afloat with no coast to tie up against.
-Black_Sea
-Red_Sea
-Persian_Gulf
-Sea_of_Okhotsk
Mariana_Islands
Hawaii
Cape_Verde
